Admonition: 'nepos' is taken as 'nephew' because the Acts call Constantine the uncle (patruus) of the emperor; it could also mean 'grandson'. 'Noella' is the edition's form, probably for the cemetery of Novella on the Via Salaria. The Admonition's 'Beroea in Syria' is given as printed; ancient accounts of Liberius's exile place Beroea in Thrace. Near the end of II, the damaged 'a(??)' is read as 'annis' (years), 'exprimere (??)na(??) est' as 'conatus est' (tried), and 'receptiorem' as 'recentiorem' (more recent), which affects the sense. Section 1: 'Anno regni' lacks a number, so one may have dropped out. 'Sacerdos' is rendered 'priest', though it here means a bishop. The editorial variant 'unus ms. quod est' (one manuscript reads 'quod est') is left out of the translation. The clause on 'unum eumdemque verum hominem' seems awkward and may be corrupt; one might expect 'true man and true God'. Section 2: the opening sentence is an anacoluthon and has no main verb; its subject is unclear. The edition's 'dele quia' is followed. 'Aquilone villa' is probably Achyron, the estate near Nicomedia where Constantine was baptized. 'Milliario in' is read as 'milliario III', as the Admonition confirms. The emperor is called Constantine, Constans and Constantius indiscriminately, as the Admonition says, and the variation is kept. Section 3: 'tyfus' is taken as 'fever', and 'vacem' as 'vocem'. The edition's suggested corrections 'chrisma' and 'oportet' are followed. Dionysius's words on the dove and the voice are obscure. Section 5: 'Juba ore meo... et infunde favore' is obscure and possibly corrupt; the rendering is tentative. The saying quoted by Liberius is a loose form of a Gospel saying. The edition's suggested 'quod' for 'quem' is followed.

Editorial readings in parentheses in the Latin are followed without comment where they are evident, including Constantius for Constans; the text prints Constans throughout 2.6 and 2.9, though the emperor meant is Constantius. 2.6: 'palmum meum' (my palm) is odd; the legend of Silvester cleansing a leprous emperor concerns Constantine, so 'patrem meum' (my father) may be meant, but the text is translated as printed. 'super quadrupedes Danubii' is obscure; 'on four-footed beasts to the Danube' is a guess. 2.7: 'sensus obscurus' is taken as Liberius's mind being darkened, and 'his uncle' seems to mean the emperor's uncle, though the sense is uncertain; a marginal note gives 'father' from the Acts of Damasus. The Latin of the sentence on the uncle's 'power' is broken. 2.8: 'munimenta' is taken as 'monumenta' (tombs); 'super aqua denatabat' is obscure. 'norum' after 'Christi' seems corrupt and is left untranslated. 'ab hora quasi' lacks its number. 2.9: the Latin moves without signal from the emperor to Liberius at 'And he sat'; the sentence on the emperor's baptism at the villa 'Aquilo' seems to confuse him with Constantine (Achyron near Nicomedia). The consular date is reported as printed, and the figures for the reign are irregular (13 months). 3.2: the print has 362 and 365, which are evident errors: Liberius became pope in 352 and the Council of Milan was in 355, so these dates are translated. 'conficiam' is read as 'confictam' (forged).

In the forged letter, the printed "Paulam" is taken as Paul (Paulum). "Exstitit" is rendered by the edition's suggested correction "exigit" ("requires"). "Unanimitatem nostram" is read as "vestram" ("your unanimity"), since the letter addresses its recipients. In the Monitum, the garbled Greek "Zwt «ρχΰν" is read as ζήτει ἀρχήν, following the Latin gloss "Quaere initium". "Argumentum eis prolixum" is odd and possibly corrupt; it is taken to mean an argument extended at length in the two letters. "Nostri" ("our colleagues") presumably refers to the Benedictine editors of Athanasius.

nodes.text: APPENDIX. THE ACTS OF POPE LIBERIUS.
ADMONITION ON THE FOLLOWING ACTS.
(Coustant, Appendix, p. 87)

I. In an old collection written out in Lombardic script, the following Acts are placed directly after the pseudo-Constitutum of Silvester. Their fabricator betrays himself from the outset as a liar and an ignoramus, when he not only calls the emperor who reigned at Rome under Pope Liberius indiscriminately Constantine, Constans and Constantius, but also names him "nephew of Constantine the Great," although it is established that this emperor's son Constantius was then ruling at Rome. Next, he repeats what is invented about Constantine's leprosy and his baptism in the false Acts of Pope Silvester and the pseudo-Constitutum. And what Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, reports about the baptism of Constantine the Great, received at Nicomedia from Eusebius, bishop of that city, he stupidly interprets as referring to the baptism of this fictitious nephew. No less falsely, he attributes to Constantius the heretical opinion about Mary's having several sons. And who would not perceive that he blunders shamefully when he sets out either the cause or the place of Liberius's exile? For Liberius was not banished by Constantius because he had mocked or accused him and said to him, "Your kingdom will not last, because you do not fear the Lord," but because he refused to subscribe to the condemnation of Athanasius. Nor is anyone unaware of this too, that he was exiled not in the cemetery of Noella, only three miles distant from the City, but at Beroea in Syria. Moreover, he presents him as staying in this cemetery as if unaware that Felix had been put in his place. And he lies that Damasus was a presbyter at the time when Liberius went into exile, and that he was made Liberius's vicar by him before he left Rome; although it is certain from the petition of Marcellinus and Faustinus to the emperors Valentinian, Theodosius and Arcadius that he was then only a deacon, and a companion of Liberius on his departure. For there, on p. 2, one may read: "Damasus his deacon pretends to set out with Liberius: then, fleeing from the journey, he returned to Rome." Surely he would have had a lawful reason for not setting out, or at least for returning sooner, if he had been appointed Liberius's vicar by the man himself. But what is added immediately in the same petition says something else entirely: "On the day on which Liberius was setting out for exile, all the clergy, that is, the presbyters, and the archdeacon Felix, and Damasus the deacon himself... affirmed under oath that, while Liberius lived, they would in no way have another pontiff. But the clergy, against what is right,... accepted the archdeacon Felix, ordained in Liberius's place." It is tiresome, however, to linger any longer over refuting such open lies, especially since the rest consists likewise either of fables, or of events wrongly understood, or related in the wrong order.

II. We suspect that the architect of these Acts is none other than the one who fabricated the Acts of Marcellinus above and the pseudo-Constitutum of Silvester. This is suggested both by the place they occupy in the handwritten copies, and by the barbarous manner of speech, though it is a little more tolerable, and also by an equal lack of skill in devising lies and an equal impudence in putting them forward. For this reason it will not be useless to add them to the aforesaid works. They will certainly serve this purpose, that it may be known from where the beginnings were taken of the Life of Damasus, which was copied by the abbot Constantino Gaetani from a manuscript codex of the archive of the Canons of St Peter's, and printed at Paris in 1672 by Louis Billaine with the other works of Pope Damasus, p. 21. For the writer of this Life, though not wholly lacking either in style or in learning, undeniably adhered to the statements of those Acts without sufficient caution. He did indeed correct many absurd and discordant things; some things, too, that were at odds with historical truth he brought back to its standard: but he did not correct everything in such a way as to leave nothing needing correction. For he did not amend what is read in these Acts about Liberius's exile in the cemetery of Noella, three miles distant from the City. And although he does not conceal that Felix was put in his place, he nevertheless represents Liberius as one who entrusts his functions to Damasus, and thereafter summons to himself "all the Catholic ecclesiastical grades," and in their presence confers baptism on many thousands, once and a second time. We pass over the fact that this same writer believed that the embassy of Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari, Pancratius and Hilary to Constantius, and also the exiles of the same Lucifer, of Eusebius of Vercelli and of Liberius himself, which preceded the Council of Rimini by three or four years, were later than this synod; that he confuses Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, with Hilary the deacon, who adhered to the Luciferian schism; and other similar things, on which this is not the place to discourse further. Here it is enough to have noted that this writer manifestly appears to be more recent than these Acts, which he tried to express in a better form.
HERE BEGIN THE ACTS OF POPE LIBERIUS.
(From the same source, p. 89.)

1. Confession of faith. — In the year of the reign of King Constantine, nephew of the great man Constantine, there was a certain priest of the City named Liberius, a pious prelate preaching Christ, as he had also been taught by Marcus, bishop of the city of Rome, who ordained him deacon in the city, in the bosom of the Constantinian basilica; he was ever fixed in the Trinity, preaching the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and praising "God from God and light from light, whole from whole, full from full; not created, but begotten; not from nothing, but from the Father, of one substance with the Father; and the Holy Spirit, our God, neither unbegotten nor begotten, neither created nor made, but proceeding from the Father, the [Spirit] of the Father and the Son, ever coeternal with the Father and the Son, we venerate; yet one God, because from the one Father, as all that is the Father's, God the Son was born, and all that is in the Father, all of it he begot as the Son. The Father, in begetting the Son, neither diminished nor lost the deity of his fullness. And confessing most certainly that all that God the Father is, the Son also is, we most piously confess, with the Holy Spirit, one God. We believe that Jesus Christ our Lord, the Son of God, through whom all things were made that are in the heavens and on earth, visible and invisible, for our salvation came down from heaven, he who never ceased to be in heaven, and was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary. The Word made flesh did not lose what he was, but began to be what he was not, not changed, but remaining God, born also a man, not in seeming but truly, not airy but bodily, not phantasmal but of flesh, having bones, blood, sense and soul; so true a man as he is true God, we in no way doubt that it must be confessed that he was one and the same true man. We [believe] that this same Lord Jesus Christ fulfilled the Law and the Prophets, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified according to the Scriptures, rose from the dead on the third day, was taken up into the heavens, sits at the right hand of the Father, and we await his coming thence to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire."

2. Constantine cleansed of leprosy. Constans baptized at Nicomedia. Liberius banished to Noella. — When he had read this from an ancient book, having been instructed by the book of Silvester, bishop of the Romans, because he also preached publicly that Constantine, uncle of Constans, had been cleansed of leprosy by Silvester in the name of Jesus Christ; for Constans was not wholly a Christian, but a sort of tempter, baptized indeed in the Trinity, yet he did not wholly confess the Trinity. He had been baptized by Eusebius of Nicomedia at Nicomedia, in the Aquilone estate. And he used to say that Joseph had other sons by Mary. When Liberius, bishop of the city of Rome, heard this, he began to mock him, and to accuse him in a clear voice, and to say with all his strength: "Your kingdom will not last, because you do not fear the Lord your God." When many reported this to King Constantius, he became very angry, and ordered him to live outside the city. So he lived three miles from the city of Rome, as if an exile, in the cemetery of Noella on the Via Salaria.

3. Liberius appoints Damasus vicar. Peter's love after his denial. Chrism in the name of the Lord. — When the day of Easter came, he called together all the presbyters who were Roman citizens and the deacons, and he sat in the same cemetery and said: "Do not fear because I do not live with you in the city of Rome, but you have a vicar; behold our brother and presbyter Damasus, to whom you bear witness to me, whom you proclaim in a clear voice in body and mind." And Dionysius the presbyter answered Liberius, bishop of the city of Rome, and said: "Holy prelate, innocent of corruption and strong for the palm of Christ, you know well that the apostle Peter was sick when he denied. A fit [of fever] came, and he denied again. The fever came a third time, and he denied. The fever went away, and he wept both bitterly and sweetly. But the physician had not yet come. The physician came after the third fever, made a remedy, and cured him. He who had failed by denying three times before the Passion is restored by loving three times after the Resurrection. Look to the remedy of chrism, the sacrament of chrism. Let not that dove accuse us, since you confect the chrism also in the name of him whom you used to preach in a clear voice. That very voice, because the voice of the Lord cannot be repeated, cannot be changed, must be heard with trembling."

4. Liberius, bishop of the city of Rome, answered and said: "Lords and holy fellow presbyters, do not take thought for tomorrow. For so the Master said: For tomorrow will take thought for itself (Matt. 6:34). For this we remind you. John baptized in the desert in repentance. It was a desert because the author of baptism had not yet come. For when he came, the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove, and remained upon the waters and upon the author of baptism, and the priest presents the sacrament that he received."

5. Baptism in a basin, a river, a marsh. — Damasus the presbyter answered and said: "Grant us to celebrate Easter. I speak in humility: for the burden that you carry upon yourself we cannot lift, because you do not know where to baptize. Baptize in the basin where the Master did. That basin is not wood, but the whole world." Liberius received this speech with great honor, and wept for joy, and said to him: "You will be a greater minister, just as he too who gave us baptism said thus to the people: Let him who is least among you become greatest." Siricius the deacon answered and said: "Give the command through my mouth, prelate, and pour forth with favor. Our fathers, in a figure of baptism, passed through the midst of the sea. So it is right to be baptized in rivers and in marshes." Bishop Liberius said: "You have spoken justly." For there was there, not far from the cemetery of Noella, the Ostrian cemetery, where the apostle Peter baptized. At that same time of Easter he baptized people of both sexes to the number of four thousand and twelve: all of whom, Romans, or from far off, and others neighbors of the Romans, desired to be baptized by him.

6. The expedition of Constantius on the Danube. At that same time there came a war on the Danube, a very great host of barbarians, about within the octave of Easter. And hearing this, Constantius said: "See this sacrilegious man: he has done what was never done, [and] has practiced a superstition of vanity. That is why this huge plague of a multitude of barbarians has come upon Romania"; and he went to the war, and set out in great bitterness, and as he went out of the city gate he said: "The sacrilegious Liberius, who said that my palm was leprous, and that it was baptized by Bishop Silvester and cleansed! When I have gone on four-footed beasts to the Danube and cut down the barbarians, I will return to the city of Rome and sacrifice his flesh to the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth; Liberius alone, and no others, so that they may not say and affirm that I am a persecutor." But while [he was] in the battle of the Danube, Constantius was hard pressed.

7. Liberius is asked to baptize in the basilica of St Peter. When the day of Pentecost came, people of both sexes, having fully made profession, were pressing for baptism for fear of persecution. And Dionysius the presbyter said: "Why do you not baptize at [the shrine of] our first pontiff, the apostle Peter?" Damasus answered and said: "Do so." But the mind of Bishop Liberius was darkened, and he said: "His uncle built this church and constructed it. Therefore he has power to pass sentence over [what is] his uncle's. Besides, no water flows there. For people of both sexes desire to be reborn, not to die on account of me alone." Dionysius the presbyter answered and said: "Let them be reborn; and if they die after baptism, they will live better in [their] blood."

8. Damasus promises fonts. Liberius baptizes at Pentecost. Damasus answered and said: "Let your heart not be sad, highest prelate: for I will give you a flowing vein of a spring." Liberius was comforted with joy at this speech, and said to him: "Go, build with the Spirit flowing abundantly; and I will come with the brothers and will adore him whom Christ left to us, who is shepherd for us." And on the third day Damasus came, Siricius came, Innocentius came, Priscus and Urbanus the deacons came to the blessed apostle Peter. For there were tombs there, and water floated above them. And Damasus held something like a council with them, and said: "Give me the works of [your] ministry, so that this water may be cleared from above the corpses of men." And he made two tunnels, and emptied that place which is on the right as one enters the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter. For there was a spring in that place which was not sufficient. And Damasus cut into the hill with his own hand. And he went in further than was customary. And he built a font. And all these reported to Bishop Liberius what had been done. And he ordered all the presbyters to assemble, and the clergy of all grades, and the faithful. And in a clear voice he said: "Peter calls his sheep. Behold, a man keeping the faith, listening to Christ and to me, a sinner, has made a fold for the sheep, and has given to my speech the sweetness of honey: for this reason I rejoice, because Peter has not let the wolf enter and lay waste his sheep. Know that I proclaim baptism in the basilica of the apostle Peter." All received this with joy. For the day of Pentecost was near. He had the monasteries assemble, and the holy people of Christ [...]. And with litanies he came to the blessed apostle Peter. And when he had entered, he gave this prayer: "God, who sent your Son and showed the creature its creator, look upon this vine, and cleanse it of thorns and thistles, and bring forth its branches in strength, and grant them the fruit of truth through our God and Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit, who lives with God the Father almighty from the ages and now and unto the ages of ages." And all the people answered: "Amen." And they entered on the Saturday of Pentecost, and the font pleased Liberius, and he wept for joy, not at all bitterly, but it seemed honeycomb to all. From the ninth hour he catechized everyone, and from about the hour already toward sunset until Pentecost Sunday he did not cease to baptize. For many pressed to be baptized, so that the Masses of the Saturday were celebrated on Pentecost Sunday at about the eighth hour. And people of both sexes were baptized, nearly eight thousand eight hundred and ten. Many at that same time desired to touch the garments of Bishop Liberius.

9. On the next day, which is Monday, all the people heard that Constantius had indeed won a victory, and in an unsound mind he was saying in a clear [voice]: "I will go to Nicomedia"; and he crossed over as far as Nicomedia, and at the villa Aquilo, where he was baptized by Eusebius of Nicomedia, he turned aside to the dogma of the Arians. In the same place he died and was buried, in the consulship of Constans, for the third time, and Constantius Augustus and Bassus, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May. And he sat in that same see of the apostle Peter for 17 years, 13 months, 8 days. In his time an apse was built in the city of Rome in the fifth region, and he rested in peace.
CRITIQUE OF THE LETTER TO THE EASTERNERS.
(Coustant, Appendix, p. 93.)

I. The antiquity of this letter is proved by the fragments of Hilary transmitted to us, and by the commentary of that same prelate appended to it. But its falsity is betrayed by its very first words. For if we listen to these, Liberius, on entering the pontificate, when he received the letter of the Easterners concerning the name of Athanasius, at once sent legates to Alexandria and summoned Athanasius to Rome, and when he refused to come, separated him from the communion of the Roman Church. That this is false is so clearly proved by the genuine letter of Liberius to the Easterners, whose authenticity no one has ever doubted, that the Easterners themselves complained to Constantius that Liberius had given no credit to that earlier letter of theirs and had suppressed it altogether, "so that the crimes of the man whom they were said to have condemned might not be evident to all." For what room would there have been for this slander, if he had really done what he is said in this letter to have done? Certainly it would have been easy for Liberius to show the injustice of this complaint, if, moved by the letter of the Easterners, he had called Athanasius to Rome and soon separated him from his communion. For it would follow from this that he had neither suppressed nor despised their letter, but had taken the greatest account of it. But Liberius, conscious that he was far from this fault, of either rashly condemning Athanasius or suppressing the letter written to him by the Easterners, first testifies that he "made known the letter of the Easterners, read it to the church, read it to the council, and answered the Easterners themselves"; then he gives this reason why he refused his assent to those who demanded the condemnation of Athanasius: because "at the same time the judgment of eighty Egyptian bishops concerning Athanasius" "opposed their petition"; and "it seemed contrary to divine law," since the number of bishops for Athanasius was greater than that of those who opposed him, "to grant" these "consent in any part."

II. Must it be said that the Easterners so forestalled the mind of Liberius as to induce him to condemn Athanasius before the letter of the 80 Egyptian bishops reached Rome? But Liberius himself testifies that this was delivered to him "at the same time" as he received the letter of the Easterners. But even if we were to suppose that the Easterners were more diligent in this matter than the Egyptian bishops, nothing at all would follow from it, unless it were also granted that Liberius, after receiving the letter of the Easterners, dispatched legates to Alexandria, and that these legates returned from Alexandria to Rome before the letter of the Egyptians was delivered to Liberius. Indeed, even then this pope ought not to have said that he had been prevented by the letter of the Egyptians from "granting consent" to the Easterners, but rather that he had been induced by it to revoke the consent already granted. We pass over the fact that Athanasius writes that Liberius, as long as he was free, could never be bent to condemn him; that the dialogue of the emperor Constantius with Liberius gives proof that up to that time Athanasius had not been condemned by him; and finally that Liberius himself, when already cast down from his zeal for defending Athanasius, shows that he had until then been constant in defending him, when he gives this reason for his constancy: "Because Julius of good memory, the bishop, my predecessor, had received him, I feared that I might be judged a transgressor by someone." Arguments of this kind, set out more fully, and some others that demonstrate the falsity of the following letter, may be seen in Hilary, fragment 4. And indeed Hilary, in the annotations that he appended to this letter, speaks of it in such a way as to show that he thought it was forged by Potamius and Epictetus, and then sent by Fortunatianus, bishop of Aquileia, to various bishops. From this it follows that it was circulated not in the year 352, when Liberius entered upon the pontificate, but after the Council of Milan held in the year 355, in which Fortunatianus fell from his former good repute.
LETTER,
IN WHICH ATHANASIUS IS FALSELY REPRESENTED AS SUMMONED TO ROME AND SEPARATED FROM THE COMMUNION OF THE ROMAN CHURCH, AND HIS EASTERN ADVERSARIES AS ADMITTED BY LIBERIUS INTO HIS COMMUNION.
(Coustant, Appendix, p. 95.)
To our most beloved brothers and fellow bishops, all those established throughout the East, Liberius, bishop of the city of Rome, [sends] eternal greeting.

Being eager for the peace and concord of the churches, after I received the letter of your charity concerning Athanasius and the others, addressed to Julius, bishop of good memory, I followed the tradition of our forebears and sent the presbyters of the city of Rome Lucius, Paul and Helianus from my side to Alexandria, to the aforesaid Athanasius, that he should come to the city of Rome, so that what the discipline of the Church requires might be decided concerning him in his presence. I also gave to the aforesaid presbyters a letter to him, in which it was stated that if he did not come, he should know that he was estranged from the communion of the Roman church. The presbyters, then, on their return reported that he had refused to come. Accordingly, following the letter of your charity which you gave us concerning the aforesaid Athanasius, know by this letter, which I have given to your unanimity, that I have peace with all of you and with all the bishops of the Catholic Church, but that the aforesaid Athanasius is estranged from my communion, that is, that of the Roman church, and from the fellowship of ecclesiastical letters.
ADMONITION
ON THE EXCHANGE OF LETTERS BETWEEN LIBERIUS AND ATHANASIUS.
(Coustant, Appendix, p. 95.)

I. In the most recent edition of the works of Athanasius, vol. 2, p. 667, our colleagues have pointed out that these two letters do indeed exist in very ancient manuscripts of Athanasius, but that, as may be conjectured from the wording, they seem to them the work of one and the same unskilled Greekling; that certainly what is asserted there concerning the Trinity is foreign to the formulas of speech customary with Athanasius; and that it is no slight argument for forgery that, amid so great a disturbance of affairs as that by which the whole Church was shaken when Liberius entered on the pontificate, no mention is made of the iniquity of the times; finally, that the first, as is indicated by a marginal note of the Coislin manuscript, in which "Seek the beginning" is written, lacks its opening, while the other displays no form of a letter at all, but is like some inept and tangled exposition of the faith.

II. To these points we add that at the head of each is set forth, as title and subject, "That God the Word assumed perfect man," although in neither of these letters does the fabricator touch on this subject, and in the first he is content to say of God the Word "who assumed perfect man without sin," while in the other he does not say even a word about the perfect man assumed. From this it is confirmed that both are mutilated. It is also easily proved that the argument itself, extended at length in them, by which the Apollinarian heresy is rejected, does not at all suit the times of Liberius, since this heresy began to be known and spread abroad in the West only under the pontificate of Damasus. But even if it had become known earlier, to what purpose should a profession of the perfect man assumed by the Word be demanded of Athanasius, who was never suspected of the Apollinarian heresy? Indeed, what is meant by "Write back to me whether you think just as we do in the true faith, so that I may be able confidently and without risk to perform what you ask"? For although Liberius, under force, defected for a time from communion with Athanasius, yet he never doubted his orthodox faith, either at the beginning of his pontificate (when he had been informed both by what had been done under Julius and by the letter of eighty Egyptian bishops) or at any other time. Nor does that laboured assertion of the divine nature of the Holy Spirit, which is found in the first letter, savour of Liberius. For since in the last period of his life he demanded from those who were afterwards called Macedonians no other profession concerning the Holy Spirit than that which is set out in the Nicene creed, how much more would he have been content with the same profession at the beginning of his pontificate.
